https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn0j.text: Image source, Getty Images By Hugh Schofield Paris correspondent Published 2 hours ago A French court has for the first time recognised cosmic radiation as a factor in the breast cancer of a long-serving flight attendant. Sophie Lainault, a 59 year-old former stewardess on Air France, sought to have her cancer recognised as an occupational disease, brought on by conditions at work. This has now been confirmed in a landmark court ruling in the southwestern town of Bayonne, which said that cosmic radiation was one of three carcinogenic hazards arising from her profession. The other two were passive smoking and prolonged night work. Smoking was authorised on Air France flights until 2000. The decision means that Lainault, who is in remission from her cancer, can take early retirement with any further treatment fully reimbursed by the French health system. And by establishing breast cancer as an officially-recognised risk for flight crews, the court has also cleared the way for many other similar claims, lawyers say. "My dearest wish is that the decision encourages other women who up until now have not had the courage to take this step," Lainault said. As stewardess and later purser on Air France airliners, Lainault clocked up 12,600 flight hours between 1989 and 2019. More than half of these were at night. Many long-distance high-altitude flights from Paris would have taken her near the North Pole, where exposure to radiation from space â strictly speaking particles from the sun and other stars â is the most intense. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Air France said that the health of its staff was "an absolute imperative" A study this month at the Harvard Medical School in the US , external found that flight attendants and pilots had the highest level of radiation-related cancer deaths among more than 500 different professions. In all, about 6.9% of deaths among flight attendants and 6.7% of deaths among pilots were from radiation-related cancers, according to the analysis. These proportions were higher than for other professions including nuclear technologists, who are routinely exposed to radiation from non-cosmic sources yet placed 12th on the list, the authors said. It has long been known that air travel at high altitudes exposes people to cosmic radiation, but the dose for most travellers is regarded as statistically insignificant , external . Exposure at the poles is more intense because elsewhere the earth's magnetic field acts as a shield. "In France the link between breast cancer and certain hazards has been established for a number of professions, such as nurses â¦ but this is the first time for an air-hostess," said Lainault's lawyer Elisabeth Leroux. Air France said it had played no part in Lainault's legal case and had not seen the reasoning behind the court's decision. "The health and security of our staff is an absolute imperative," it said. "Every employee has a medical accompaniment that goes well beyond the regulatory minimum." President Xi Jinping called for urgent search and rescue efforts and a swift investigation. Premier Li Qiang called for "trapped" people to be rescued and stressed the need to "prevent secondary disasters". The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze occurred at 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT), state news agency Xinhua said. https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/.text: The Hungarian government has published a 220-page, comprehensive child-protection report which concluded that the child adoption system is on the verge of collapse.The document will serve as the basis for rewriting adoption rules, a move that has triggered fierce political reactions among opposition parties.Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that the government will change the regulations governing adoption by single persons and same-sex couples, arguing that the current system is unsustainable.He stated that deciding who may adopt a child should not be a political decision but one taken by professionals, like psychologists and child-protection experts. Politicians, Magyar said, need to take a step back from this issue.He stressed that the "system cannot function properly in its current state," and that the overpowering consideration must always be that children can grow up in a loving family, not the parents' sexual orientation or marital status.The Hungarian premier said the government is already working on amendments to the existing legislation, which was introduced earlier by Fidesz under longtime Prime Minister and Magyar's predecessor, Viktor Orbán.The system Magyar wants to overhaul, in its current state, favours married couples and severely restricts the options available to single people and same-sex couples.The announcement has generated strong criticism in local media, with opposition outlets slamming the move, accusing Magyar of "giving in to the LGBTQ lobby", while independent media reported it as a pledge to restore professional standards.Policy break from Orbán-eraThe move marks a sharp ideological and policy break with the legacy of the Orbán governments in power between 2010 and 2026, and is one of the most significant steps taken yet on human rights and child protection in Hungary since the change of government in April 2026.In December 2020, the Orbán government tightened the Hungarian Fundamental Law and the adoption act, which tightly defined a mother as a biological female and the father a biological male, effectively restricting adoption to married couples as the default.Because same-sex couples in Hungary cannot marry, and can only enter into registered partnerships, they had previously been able to adopt by having one partner submit the application as a single person.A 2020 law ended this loophole, as it forced single applicants to adopt only with a valid personal ministerial permit, initially granted by former President Katalin Novák and later by the minister responsible for family policy.The amended legislation effectively blocked members of the LGBTQ community almost entirely from the possibility of having children.After the Tisza Party won the elections in April this year by a landslide, thereby ending Fidesz's 16 years in power, international and domestic human rights organisations expected immediate steps to restore LGBTQ rights.Pressure increased further when, just before the vote, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Hungary's earlier "child-protection/homophobic" law seriously breaches EU law.According to the government's narrative, the current system is unsustainable because, while large numbers of children live in state-care, suitable prospective parents, whether single or in same-sex relationships, are blocked in the system due to strict political filters and bureaucratic hurdles.The new measure effectively restores the pre-2020, profession-based assessment system and sends a strong signal that the new government intends to approach social issues, previously used as symbolic political battlegrounds, in a pragmatic, expert-led way.

https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/14/m.text: Coerced sex or a jealous ex? Jury weighs dueling accounts of star scientist David Sabatini’s downfall. David Sabatini listened Wednesday to closing arguments in a pair of lawsuits that were tried over three weeks in Boston. David L. Ryan/Globe Staff Was world-renowned molecular biologist David Sabatini a manipulative mentor who coerced a younger colleague into sex and cultivated a hostile work culture at his research lab in Cambridge? Or was he the victim of a spurned former lover and a #MeToo movement gone too far? A dozen jurors in Boston are weighing these starkly opposing interpretations following a bruising, three-week civil trial that exposed the intense power dynamics and permissive sexual norms inside the world-famous Whitehead Institute , where Sabatini ran his own laboratory. Standing between the jury and a verdict are scores of hours of conflicting testimony, bitter recriminations, and a vast trove of unfiltered texts exchanged by two brilliant scientists. The yearslong feud offers a rare window into the insular world of top-tier science labs, where directors wield outsized authority. It also highlights a broader challenge confronting modern workplaces: How to maintain professional boundaries within close-knit, diverse teams as behavioral standards evolve. Tall and gangly, with unruly black hair, Sabatini vaulted into scientific stardom as a graduate student at the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. His groundbreaking discovery of mTOR — a key protein regulating cell growth — yielded vital insights into aging and cancer while generating Nobel buzz. He spent the next two decades directing a high-powered lab at Whitehead, managing up to 40 researchers and a $5 million annual budget. That promising career unraveled in 2021. An internal investigation concluded Sabatini had violated Whitehead’s policy on workplace relationships through an affair with Kristin Knouse , a much younger colleague whose career he was in a position to influence. While investigators and several former lab members described his lab as a toxic and sexually charged environment, others fiercely disputed those claims, praising Sabatini’s mentorship and inspiration. Sabatini’s downfall — chronicled in a 2023 report from The Boston Globe Spotlight Team — sent shockwaves through the scientific community, triggering condemnation in academia and a campus walkout at a prestigious medical school. Observers split into opposing camps: those who viewed Sabatini as the victim of a smear campaign fueled by #MeToo excesses, and those who welcomed his removal as part of an overdue reckoning. In a lawsuit filed five years ago, Sabatini says he and Knouse began a consensual sexual relationship in 2018. He alleges that after the relationship ended, Knouse aggressively sought to resume it and then made false and defamatory statements about him. He also alleges Whitehead relied on a biased investigation to force him out, costing him his laboratory, research funding, and a potential new job. Knouse countersued, asserting Sabatini abused his position of power by subjecting her to a coerced, nonconsensual relationship and a highly sexualized work culture. “There’s a straight line here, and the straight line moves from Dr. Sabatini’s conduct to the consequences he complains of,” Ellen Zucker , Knouse’s attorney, said in court Wednesday. “It’s a straight line. There were rules. He broke them.” After closing arguments Wednesday, both suits are now in the hands of a Suffolk County jury. Deliberations are due to continue Friday, a lawyer said. On the trial’s final day, the two accusers sat less than 20 feet apart: Knouse, bolt upright near the front, and Sabatini — in a navy suit and burgundy tie — appearing relaxed in the back of the courtroom, taking notes and occasionally fanning himself. The jury now faces the daunting task of parsing thousands of pages of court filings and a massive trail of often-explicit texts between the two star researchers. The exchanges frequently related to where the pair would meet for drinks and sex encounters they often referred to as “consults” in texts. Both sides have cited the texts to support their claims: Sabatini to argue Knouse pursued him and became increasingly more engaged with him, and Knouse to support her counterclaim that he fostered a sexually explicit workplace. The two initially bonded over their shared love of science — he had been her teacher and mentor — and good whiskey. Their connection turned intimate during a 2018 conference in Washington, D.C. At the time, Knouse was about to begin as a Whitehead Fellow, part of a program in which young scientists are given seed money to start their own labs. Sabatini and Knouse met up and each posted photos on Twitter of the various whiskies they tasted. What is undisputed is this: They ended up in Sabatini’s hotel room that night and had sex. But Sabatini characterizes the sexual encounter as consensual. Knouse alleges she tried resisting his advances and was coerced. The next day, Knouse texted Sabatini about having gone for a run in the morning and expressed no regrets about their night together, according to Sabatini’s attorneys. Four days later, on April 22, the pair debated by email the merits of various whiskeys and discussing how to acquire rare bottles. Sabatini’s legal team contends Knouse’s conduct demonstrates the encounter was entirely consensual. “Was it stupid for [Sabatini] to have sex with her?” his attorney, Lisa Arrowood , asked the jury Wednesday. “Absolutely. The biggest mistake of his life. But was it rape? Absolutely not.” The two continued a secret relationship for roughly a year and a half, having sex about 10 to 15 times while maintaining a friendship, according to accounts they later gave to investigators. They also spent time together outside work, and Sabatini mentored her as she started her lab, the Globe previously reported. However, their accounts of that period diverge sharply. Sabatini described the arrangement as a casual friendship with occasional sex, adding he believed Knouse began seeking a deeper commitment in 2019. Knouse told investigators she felt anxious about Sabatini’s professional influence from the start, eventually feeling sexually exploited and emotionally used. By late 2019, the relationship had grown strained. When Sabatini told her in January 2020 that he wanted to pursue another scientist, the two ended their affair. Their relationship had begun against the backdrop of the #MeToo movement , which drew national scrutiny to sexual harassment and abuses of power in the workplace and called for holding perpetrators accountable. Across the country, human resources departments were grappling with how to draft policies that acknowledged the reality of workplace attraction while safeguarding employees from exploitation. In August 2018, five months after the encounters between Sabatini and Knouse began, the Whitehead Institute amended its rules to take an unusually hard stand against consensual relationships. It banned faculty members, senior managers, and principal investigators from having sexual relationships with any Whitehead employee, even peers. After receiving complaints about Sabatini, including from Knouse, Whitehead hired an independent legal team to investigate. The investigators found he “engaged in and otherwise tolerated sexist and sexualized work discussions” in his lab, and that taking part in those discussions was “an implicit part of succeeding” there. They concluded that he had violated Whitehead’s ban on sexual harassment. Sabatini resigned in August 2021, and the next year from his tenured position at MIT. Before long, Sabatini drew the attention of the #MeToo movement. In early 2022, about 200 graduate students, faculty, and alumni from New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine staged a walkout after learning he might be hired at the school. Many held handmade signs with slogans like “No means no” and “Students Against Sabatini!” Shunned by academia, Sabatini sank into a deep depression — struggling to eat or sleep, and eventually attempting suicide, according to court testimony. At times, he became emotional on the stand. He maintains the allegations cost him $1.9 million in lost income between 2020 and 2025. In her counterclaim, Knouse alleged Sabatini operated as if he were above the rules, fostering an environment in his lab where researchers felt pressured to participate in a sexualized culture to advance their careers. According to the filing, talk about sex was commonplace, and Sabatini routinely attempted to draw female researchers into unwelcome conversations about their intimate lives. “He sought out young women he believed were attractive for grooming, and he shamed individuals who had the temerity not to play along,” Knouse alleges. In 2023, New York hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman and an anonymous donor pledged $25 million over five years to help Sabatini get back into science. Sabatini accepted a position as a group leader with a laboratory in the Czech Republic , where he continues to focus on topics related to growth, metabolism, and aging. Knouse is currently an assistant professor of biology at MIT and a faculty member of its Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research. Chris Serres can be reached at chris.serres@globe.com . Follow him @ChrisSerres .

https://hotnews.ro/bolojenistul-din-psd-.text: Sorin Grindeanu îi reproșează primarului Buzăului, Constantin Toma, că stă „de dimineața până seara pe la televiziuni”, în loc să se ocupe de administrație, și îl acuză că a pierdut 80 de milioane de euro din PNRR. Criticile au fost făcute de liderul PSD la începutul ședinței de luni a conducerii partidului. „O felicit pe Olguța Vasilescu pentru proiectul de peste 500 de milioane de euro, inaugurat la Craiova, prin care craiovenii au acum apă de izvor de munte la robinet! A demonstrat că știe să atragă fonduri, spre deosebire de domnul Toma de la Buzău, care stă de dimineața până seara pe la televiziuni să-și prezinte opiniile politice, dar a pierdut 80 de milioane de euro din PNRR pentru anveloparea blocurilor. Deci Olguța a atras bani europeni, în timp ce Toma a pierdut zeci de milioane de euro. Asta înseamnă să fii preocupat de oameni și nu de analize politice. Aici e diferența”, a spus Grindeanu, potrivit surselor participante la discuții. Primarul Buzăului, Constantin Toma, este unul dintre liderii social-democrați care au criticat deschis conducerea actuală a partidului. El a susținut că moțiunea de cenzură împotriva Guvernului Bolojan a fost o greșeală. Preşedintele PNL, Ilie Bolojan, a dezvăluit, vineri, în faţa liberalilor din Buzău, că la prânz l-a vizitat la primărie pe primarul PSD Constantin Toma, la invitația acestuia. Fostul premier a ţinut să lămurească imediat că vizita nu are nicio semnificaţie politică. HotNews.ro utilizează cookie-uri pentru a îmbunătăți experiența dvs .
